Pulse for 9 November 2026

The stories from 9 November 2026 in the Pulse of the Sapaude app, in our own words. Terms you don’t know are explained in the glossary. Glossary

Everyday tool

Antigravity for non-coders

Google has added a Knowledge Work layout to its Antigravity agent app. It hides Git, diffs and terminals for people who use the app for research, documents and analysis, while the agent underneath stays the same.

New model

Claude Fable 5.2 is out

Anthropic has released Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2, two versions of one model for the hardest technical work. The company says they write up to 30 percent faster than the 5.1 models and cost less.

New model

Meta launches Muse Ember

Meta Superintelligence Labs has released Muse Ember, its smallest and most efficient model, built for the steps agents repeat all day: tool calls, coding subtasks, routing, extraction and long documents.

Everyday tool

Ask AI inside your draft

TK is a free writing app from Medium that puts an assistant inside the document, so you type @TK and a request instead of opening another tab.

Everyday tool

3D models, made in ChatGPT

Autodesk has put its Flow Studio 3D tool into ChatGPT as a plugin: a text prompt or a reference image becomes a 3D asset that lands in your Flow Studio library.

Everyday tool

AI checks Instagram ages

Meta is rolling out its AI age estimation on Instagram worldwide. Accounts the system suspects belong to teens move into Teen Account protections, even if they were opened with an adult birthday.

Device

Google adds two new TPUs

Google has added TPU 8tx and TPU 8i Max to its eighth TPU generation: one keeps data and model weights protected even while they are being processed, the other targets very large context windows.

New model

Image edits that hold still

ByteDance's new image model Seedream 5.5 is meant to change only what you ask for, even after 100 edits to the same picture, and to deliver cut-outs with a transparent background.

New model

AI simulates many materials

WorldParticle is a research model from MIT and the University of British Columbia that predicts the next move of tiny particles, so one system can stand in for separate hand-built simulators for sand, fluids, and proteins.
